texts.160g-gA-fixed:
In 2023 the Zapatistas went through a long internal review and announced they were dissolving the Rebel Zapatista Autonomous Municipalities and the Good Government Juntas, and moving authority toward a more local level, a Local Autonomous Government in each community, which can coordinate through regional collectives, but making clear that the coordinating levels depend on the communities and aren't above them.

In most institutions, as time goes on, more and more layers and offices are added, but in their review the Zapatistas took the opposite approach and pushed authority downward. And did they publish a book on leadership, and then open a certification program? Nope. They simply changed the system they were actually living in.

Also, I need to restrain my enthusiasm here. This level of autonomy is born out of communities with long histories (Indigenous communities that share language, family ties, long struggles for land, and decades of defending themselves together). So a new ecovillage can't just "copy" the visible diagram and instantly have the trust underneath it.

Additionally, the Zapatistas themselves warn people not to import or export Zapatismo as a ready-made model. What's useful to "import" isn't their diagram. It's how they learn: building and asking questions, finding out where the practice fails, and changing the structure.

The Zapatistas also don't prove my whole economic path, from unpriced internal necessities, to a common purse, to eventually eliminating outside money altogether. Zapatista communities do use collective work for their schools and clinics, and for their autonomous government and resistance, but they also produce things for sale and engage in trade, and they get support from outside. What they do show is that it is possible for a community to take major necessities and public functions out of ordinary market purchase, and govern them collectively. It may be helpful to bring in outside help to build capacities, but if the specialist or donor or organization providing the help stays indispensable, it can also create gatekeepers and uneven dependence.

texts.160g-gB-fixed:
In the context of this research I have also looked for evidence of the long-term impact of the Escuelita. While I found information on alumni networks, people bringing practices back with them, and organizing later, I couldn't find a clear chain of somebody having been to the Escuelita, then setting up a new communal institution, and then evidence about how its members and their children actually did over time. Zapatista influence was already spreading abroad before the Escuelita, so if some institution resembles a Zapatista one later, that alone doesn't prove the Escuelita was responsible. Nonetheless I'm borrowing their teaching method and their ambition to replicate, not claiming they already proved my whole model.

Sociocracy has a very different history, yet it also ended up with some similar forms: circles, decision-making by consent, distributed authority and ways of connecting the levels. Does this prove that there is one universal formula for this? No. But it gives people who want to build something similar another serious system to study, instead of inventing their governance during their first dispute.

texts.160g-gB-fix17:
In the context of this research I have looked for evidence of the long-term impact of the Escuelita. While I found plenty of information of people networking, bringing practice back with them and organising, I couldn’t find evidence of the causal chain of somebody having been to the Escuelita, then setting up a communal institution and then good evidence about how well its members and their children have done. As I have also found evidence of Zapatista influence abroad before the Escuelita, it’s hard to prove that the Escuelita was responsible for some other institutions resembling Zapatista institutions. Nonetheless I’m trying their teaching method of “try this and see if it works for, if it does, try to replicate” rather than “first prove it works and then try to convince others”.

Sociocracy has a very different history, yet it also ended up with some similar forms: circles, decision-making by consent, distributed authority and ways of connecting the levels. Does this prove that there is one universal formula for this? No. But it gives people who want to build something similar another serious system to study, instead of inventing their governance during their first dispute.
